- `enable --agent ... --force` does reinstall hooks, because both `enable` and `configure` route `--agent` through [setupAgentHooksNonInteractive](/Users/soph/Work/entire/devenv/cli/cmd/entire/cli/setup.go:1137), which passes `opts.ForceHooks` into `setupAgentHooks(...)`.

- `entire configure --agent claude-code --force` rewrites a stale Claude hook

I think your direction is sound. The real brittle part is that `enable` and `configure` currently reimplement overlapping setup logic with slightly different branches, and the `--force` bug came from one of those branches drifting.

The clean rule is:

- `entire enable` with no setup/configuration flags should mean “flip enabled back on”.
- Any `enable` invocation that is trying to mutate setup state should reuse the `configure` path.

That is broader than just `--agent`. On an already configured repo, the flags that are really “configuration” are `--agent`, `--force`, `--local-dev`, `--skip-push-sessions`, `--checkpoint-remote`, `--absolute-git-hook-path`, and the strategy flags. `--local` / `--project` are the only awkward ones because `enable` uses them as “where do I write the enabled bit”, while `configure` uses them as “where do I persist config changes”.

So my recommendation is:

- Keep `entire enable` and `entire enable --project/--local` as the re-enable-only path.
- Route `enable` into the shared configure/setup handler whenever any real setup-mutation flag is present.

That gives you the semantics you want without breaking the useful “counter to disable” behavior.

If you want, I can make that refactor now by:
1. extracting the shared configure/setup decision tree into one helper,
2. making `enable` call that helper for setup-mutation flags,
3. leaving bare `enable` and `enable --project/--local` on the existing `runEnable(...)` path,
4. adding tests that `enable --force` now follows configure behavior instead of silently doing nothing.

Yes. That’s the right direction.

`enable` currently has one legitimate special case that `configure` should not subsume: “just turn Entire back on”, which is what `runEnable(...)` does today. Everything else is setup/config mutation and is safer if it shares the `configure` code path.

I’d keep it like this:

- `entire enable`
- `entire enable --local`
- `entire enable --project`

Those stay on the simple re-enable path.

Everything else on `enable` should reuse the `configure`/setup logic:
- `--agent`
- `--force`
- `--local-dev`
- `--checkpoint-remote`
- `--skip-push-sessions`
- `--absolute-git-hook-path`
- strategy-related flags

That avoids the drift that caused this bug. It also makes the semantics clearer: `enable` is for enabled/disabled state unless you’re explicitly asking it to mutate setup, in which case it behaves like `configure`.

`--local` / `--project` are the main reason not to blindly route all `enable` calls through `configure`, because on `enable` they mean “where should the enabled bit be written”, while on `configure` they mean “where should config changes be persisted”.
